title: Lay meditation
hookLine: Ledi Sayadaw in Burma teaches meditation to laypeople, not only monks

cards: Who is meditation for? In Burma, in Ledi Sayadaw's day, the usual answer, as accounts tell it, was the monks. Lay people offered food, kept the precepts, made merit, and left the long hours of sitting to those in robes.
Ledi Sayadaw, a learned monk, started giving a different answer. Farmers could do this. Shopkeepers could.
Parents with no spare time could. He wrote short guides in plain Burmese and sent them out into the towns and villages.

teach.h: A FEAR THE PRACTICE WOULD SHRINK.
teach.b: First, the worry behind it. Accounts describe a teacher afraid the practice could shrink into something people only read about, kept alive by a few. His answer was to put it in more hands, not fewer.
His practical guides, in the language people actually spoke, covered keeping attention on the breath and seeing body and mind change from moment to moment.

The Pali word for that seeing is vipassana: insight, seeing clearly. It wasn't a new teaching; the instructions on mindfulness of breathing and of the body are in the old suttas. What was new was who he handed them to.
A story told in this lineage: a rice farmer named Saya Thetgyi learned from Ledi and became a teacher himself, a lay man teaching lay people in his own village.

From him the teaching passed through other lay teachers, and teachers in this line say it now reaches meditation halls far from Burma, where lay people of every kind sit side by side. Fourth, what changed and what didn't.
Ledi didn't set monastic life aside; he stayed a monk.

He simply said the door was wider than people thought. Sitting wasn't a reward for leaving the world. It was something to carry into it, between the fields and the market, between one chore and the next.

how: In Theravada countries and beyond, lay Buddhists now attend meditation retreats and centers, and some lineages trace this lay practice back through teachers such as Ledi Sayadaw and Saya Thetgyi.

games.q: you're Ledi Sayadaw. you fear the practice will be kept by a few and slowly fade. what do you do?
o: train more monks, and only monks.
write plain guides for anyone who can read them.
stop teaching and practice alone in the forest.
games.why: he wrote short guides in plain Burmese and taught lay people, and a farmer he taught became a teacher himself.

practice: Sit comfortably, breathe through the nose, and notice the touch of the air just at the nostrils as it comes in and as it goes out; that's the whole instruction. When the mind wanders off, come back to the touch.
Keep it simple enough that you could explain it to anyone in one sentence.

wordCard.voice: Lay meditation. Ledi Sayadaw's teaching that insight practice belongs to farmers and shopkeepers as well as monks. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali vipassana: insight, seeing clearly. the practice Ledi Sayadaw opened to lay people.

carryVoice: Your line: for everyone. The door was wider than people thought. Go gently.
